name: Variables and Types
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: How Python stores values: binding, types, conversion, mutability, aliasing, equality and truthiness, compared with JavaScript.

lesson.intro: A variable is a name bound to a value, and every value has a type that decides what you can do with it. This lesson builds that mental model: assignment, numbers, conversion, mutability, aliasing, equality and truthiness, in Python and JavaScript.
objectives: Explain assignment as binding a name and predict the effect of rebinding
Convert between str, int, float and bool and predict truncation, rounding and ValueError
Tell mutable from immutable types and avoid aliasing bugs with shallow and deep copies
Choose between == and is, and predict the truthiness of common values
Carry these ideas into JavaScript, including where it differs from Python

sections.title: Names point to values
sections.key: A variable is a name bound to a value: `y = x` gives the same value a second name, and rebinding x later never changes y.
sections.body:
Write `price = 5` and Python creates the int 5 and ties the name `price` to it. A **variable** is a name bound to a value, like a label on an object, not a box holding a copy.

[[visual]]

Tying a name to a value is **binding**; pointing it at a new value is **rebinding**, and that never affects other names.

Python is **dynamically typed**: the type belongs to the value, not the name. `x` can refer to an int now and a string later, and `type(x)` reports what it refers to right now.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Tracing three lines
visual.caption: Only the x label moved, so y still refers to 5.

visual.title: Assignment forms
rows: Binds several names at once (tuple unpacking)
Swaps: the whole right side is evaluated first, then both names are rebound
Shorthand for `count = count + 1`; also `-=`, `*=` and friends
Binds both names to the same value

items.title: Rules
points: Cannot be a keyword such as `class` or `for`

sections.code:
x = 5
y = x  # y is bound to the same 5
x = x + 1  # x is rebound to a new value, 6
print(x, y)  # 6 5

x = "five"  # the name x can refer to any type
print(type(x))  # <class 'str'>

a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a  # swap: the right side is evaluated first
print(a, b)  # 2 1
sections.pitfall: Thinking `y = x` makes a copy. It binds a second name to the same object. With numbers and strings that is harmless, since they cannot change, but with lists it causes aliasing bugs.

check.question: You run x = 10, then y = x, then x = 20. What is y now?
check.explanation: y = x bound y to the object 10. x = 20 rebinds only the name x to a new object, so y still refers to 10.

sections.title: Numbers: int, float and precision
sections.key: Ints are exact with no size limit, but floats are binary approximations, so `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is False: compare floats with `math.isclose()`.
sections.body:
Add ten cents and twenty cents in Python and you get `0.30000000000000004`. That is not a Python bug: nearly every language stores decimals this way.

[[visual]]

Most decimal fractions, like 0.1, have no exact binary form, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal form. The float stores the nearest binary value, and tiny errors appear when you combine them.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

`bool` is a kind of int: `True` acts as 1 and `False` as 0. So `True + True` is 2, and `sum()` of a list of bools counts the Trues.

items.title: int
points: Whole numbers with no size limit
`2 ** 100` is computed exactly, digit for digit
Many languages cap integers at 64 bits; Python does not

items.title: float
points: Numbers with a fractional part, stored in 64-bit binary

visual.title: Living with float error
rows: Whole cents as ints (`1999` for $19.99), or `Decimal("0.1")` built from a string

visual.title: What type comes out
rows: `3`, `1`: ints when both sides are ints
`3.0`: mixing int and float gives a float

sections.code:
import math
from decimal import Decimal

print(2 ** 100)  # 1267650600228229401496703205376
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)  # False
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))  # True
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))  # 0.3

price_cents = 1999  # $19.99, stored exactly
print(f"${price_cents * 3 / 100:.2f}")  # $59.97
print(True + True)  # 2
sections.pitfall: Testing floats with `==`. A total built by adding prices may be 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. Use `math.isclose()`, or keep money in integer cents.

check.question: What does 6 / 3 evaluate to?
check.explanation: / is true division and always returns a float, even when the result is a whole number. Use 6 // 3 to get the int 2.

sections.title: Converting between types
sections.key: Python never converts between text and numbers for you: call `int()`, `float()` or `str()` yourself, and remember that `int()` truncates toward zero.
sections.body:
A CSV file gives you `"19.99"` and a form gives you `"42"`. Both are strings, and Python will not guess: `"3" + 3` raises TypeError. You convert by calling the type you want, which is called **casting**.

[[visual]]

`int()` **truncates toward zero**: `int(-2.7)` is -2, while `math.floor(-2.7)` is -3 because flooring always rounds down.

Convert once, at the edge where data comes in (keyboard, files, network), and use proper types everywhere else. A number that is secretly a string causes bugs far from where it entered.

visual.title: Conversions and their surprises
rows: `"10"` (an f-string such as `f"{n} items"` often reads better)
`9`, `-2`: the fraction is dropped, not rounded
`2`, `4`: exact halves go to the even number (banker's rounding)
The right way to read a yes or no setting

sections.code:
print(int("42") + 1)  # 43
print(float("19.99"))  # 19.99
print(str(10) + "0")  # 100
print(int(-2.7))  # -2  (truncates toward zero)
print(round(2.5), round(3.5))  # 2 4  (halves go to the even number)
print(bool("False"))  # True  (a non-empty string)

text = "False"
flag = text.lower() == "true"
print(flag)  # False
sections.pitfall: Using `bool()` to parse text. `bool("False")` and `bool("0")` are both True. Compare the text instead.

check.question: What does int(9.99) return?
check.explanation: int() truncates a float by dropping everything after the decimal point, so 9.99 becomes 9. Use round(9.99) if you want 10.

sections.title: Mutable and immutable values
sections.key: Mutable objects (list, dict, set) change in place and those methods return None; immutable ones (int, str, tuple) never change, so keep the new value.
sections.body:
You call `name.upper()` and name does not change, but `scores.append(70)` does change scores. The difference is whether the object can change after it is created.

[[visual]]

For immutable values, keep the result: `name = name.upper()`. For mutable ones, `append()`, `sort()`, `reverse()` and `extend()` change the object and return `None`, so `nums = nums.sort()` replaces your list with None.

A **tuple** is an immutable list: `point = (3, 4)`. Reading `point[0]` works, but `point[0] = 5` raises TypeError. Because it cannot change, a tuple can be a dict key and a list cannot.

[[visual 2]]

items.title: Immutable
points: int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset, None
Safe to share: nobody can change it under you

items.title: Mutable
points: list, dict, set, and most objects of your own classes
list, dict and set cannot be dict keys

visual.title: `+=` depends on the type
rows: A new string is built and s is rebound
The old value: t is still `"ab"`
The same list is extended in place
visual.caption: Starting from `s = "ab"` and `a = [1]`.

sections.code:
s = "hi"
s.upper()
print(s)  # hi   (the new string was thrown away)
s = s.upper()
print(s)  # HI

nums = [3, 1, 2]
result = nums.sort()
print(nums, result)  # [1, 2, 3] None

point = (3, 4)
# point[0] = 5  # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
sections.deeper: Why have immutable types at all? They are safe to share: if ten parts of a program refer to the same string, none of them can change it under the others. They also keep dictionaries reliable. A dict finds a key by its hash, and a key whose value changed after it was stored would hash differently and could never be found again. That is why Python refuses lists as keys but accepts tuples of immutable values.
sections.pitfall: `nums = nums.sort()` or `nums = nums.append(4)` sets nums to None. In-place methods return None, so call them on their own line.

check.question: Which of these types is mutable?
check.explanation: Lists can be changed in place with append(), remove(), item assignment and so on. A tuple looks like a list but is immutable, like str and int.

sections.title: Aliasing and copies
sections.key: Assignment and argument passing never copy, so two names for one mutable object see each other's changes: copy with `.copy()`, or `copy.deepcopy()` for nested data.
sections.body:
A function works out a discounted cart, and afterwards the original cart is discounted too. That is **aliasing**: after `b = a`, both names are **aliases** for one object, so a change made through b shows through a.

[[visual]]

Arguments work the same way: a function that runs `items.append("x")` changes the caller's list. Prefer returning a new value, or make the change obvious from the function's name.

**Rebinding is not mutating.** `b = [9]` points b at a new list and leaves a alone. Only changes to the object itself (append, item assignment, `+=` on a list, sort) show through other names.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: One list, two names
visual.caption: After `b = a` and `b.append(4)` there is still only one list, so printing a shows the 4 too.

visual.title: How deep does the copy go?
rows: New: copied all the way down

points: Repeats one reference to a single inner list

items.title: `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]`
points: Builds a new row each time

sections.code:
import copy

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a  # an alias, not a copy
b.append(4)
print(a)  # [1, 2, 3, 4]

board = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
shallow = board.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(board)
board[0][0] = 9
print(shallow)  # [[9, 0], [0, 0]]  (inner lists are shared)
print(deep)  # [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
sections.pitfall: Assuming `.copy()` makes nested lists independent too. A shallow copy shares the inner lists; use `copy.deepcopy()` for nested data.

check.question: You run x = [0], then y = x, then y = [9]. What is x now?
check.explanation: y = [9] rebinds y to a brand-new list. Nothing happened to the list x refers to, so x is still [0]. Only mutating the shared list, for example y.append(9), would show up in x.

sections.title: Equality versus identity
sections.key: `==` asks whether two values are equal and `is` asks whether they are the very same object; use `is` mainly to check for None.
sections.body:
Two students hand in identical essays: equal content, but two separate pieces of paper. Python draws the same line.

[[visual]]

Every object has an **identity**, shown by `id(x)` and fixed for its lifetime. `a is b` is True exactly when `id(a) == id(b)`.

Use `is` for one job: `if result is None:`. It is precise, because a class can redefine `==`.

Do not use `is` for numbers or strings. CPython reuses some small ints and short strings, so `is` may seem to work in a quick test and fail later. Python even warns about `x is 5`.
sections.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b)  # True False  (equal values, two objects)
print(a == c, a is c)  # True True   (one object, two names)
print(id(a) == id(c))  # True

result = None
print(result is None)  # True: the standard None check
sections.deeper: For your own classes, `==` falls back to identity unless you define an `__eq__` method, so two `Point(1, 2)` objects are not equal until you say what equal means. The Object-Oriented Programming topic covers `__eq__` and its partner `__hash__`.
sections.pitfall: `if x == None` usually works, but `if x is None` is the idiom. `if not x` is a different test that is also true for 0, `""` and `[]`.

check.question: Which comparison should you use to test whether a variable holds None?
check.explanation: None is a single object, so an identity check is exact and is the standard style. == None depends on the class's __eq__, not x is also true for 0 and empty values, and === is JavaScript, not Python.

sections.title: None and truthiness
sections.key: `None`, `False`, zero and empty containers are falsy; everything else, including `"0"`, `" "` and `[0]`, is truthy.
sections.body:
A lookup function returns nothing for an unknown code, and three lines later `100 - discount` crashes with TypeError. **None** is Python's single "nothing here" value, of type `NoneType`. A function that ends without `return` returns None, and so do in-place methods like `list.sort()`.

Every value can be used as a condition:

[[visual]]

So `if items:` checks that a list is not empty, and `if not name:` catches an empty string.

`or` and `and` return one of their operands, not just True or False:

- `name or "Guest"` gives the first truthy operand (or the last one): a fallback when name is empty.
- `user and user.name` gives the first falsy operand (or the last one), so `.name` is read only when there is a user.
sections.code:
def greet():
    print("hi")

result = greet()  # prints hi
print(result)  # None

name = ""
print(name or "Guest")  # Guest

quantity = 0
if quantity is None:  # 0 is a real answer here, so test for None
    quantity = 1
print(quantity)  # 0
sections.pitfall: Using `x or default` when x can legitimately be 0 or empty: `quantity or 1` turns a real 0 into 1. Test `is None` instead.

activity.title: Sort truthy from falsy
activity.prompt: Predict which values are truthy before you run it. Then add if v: inside the loop so only the truthy ones are printed. repr() shows quotes around strings, so you can see the space.

props.task: Print repr(v) only for the truthy values. The output should be four lines: 1, '0', [0] and ' '.

check.question: Which of these values is truthy?
check.explanation: "0" is a non-empty string, and every non-empty string is truthy, whatever it contains. 0.0, the empty string and None are all falsy.

sections.title: Python and JavaScript side by side
sections.key: The model carries over to JavaScript, but `const` freezes only the binding, `===` replaces `==`, and empty arrays and objects are truthy.
sections.body:
Most developers work in more than one language, and Python and JavaScript are the most common pair. The ideas carry over; the details below cause real bugs when you switch.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

JavaScript's falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `[]` and `{}`, so check `arr.length === 0` instead of `!arr`.

**What stays the same:** strings are immutable, arrays and objects are mutable, and assignment creates aliases. Copy an array with `[...arr]` or `arr.slice()` (both shallow), and nested data with `structuredClone(obj)`.

visual.title: Where JavaScript surprises you
rows: Works: `const` blocks rebinding, not changes to the array
`true`: `==` converts types first, so always use `===`
`"33"`, `9`: JavaScript converts where Python raises TypeError

sections.code:
const nums = [1, 2];
nums.push(3);  // a const binding to a mutable array
console.log(nums);  // [1, 2, 3]

console.log(0 == "", 0 === "");  // true false
console.log(Boolean([]), Boolean(""));  // true false
console.log("3" + 3, "3" * 3);  // 33 9
sections.deeper: JavaScript's `number` holds whole numbers exactly only up to 2^53 - 1 (`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, about 9 quadrillion). Beyond that it rounds silently, which bites with large database ids. For bigger integers there is a separate `bigint` type written with a trailing n, such as `10n`, and you cannot mix it with ordinary numbers in arithmetic without converting.
sections.pitfall: Checking for an empty array with `if (!arr)` in JavaScript. Empty arrays are truthy there, so the check never fires. Use `arr.length === 0`.

check.question: In JavaScript you run const nums = [1, 2]; then nums.push(3);. What happens?
choices: nums stays [1, 2] because const arrays are frozen
push returns a new array and nums is unchanged
check.explanation: const stops you from rebinding the name (nums = [] would fail), but the array itself is mutable, so push changes it in place. Object.freeze() is what makes an array read-only.

keyTerms.definition: A name bound to a value. Assignment binds the name; it never copies the value.
Pointing a name at a different object. It never affects other names.
Types belong to values, not names, so one name can refer to values of different types over time.
Converting a value to another type explicitly, as in int("42") or str(42).
Tiny inaccuracies because most decimals, such as 0.1, have no exact binary form.
Can be changed in place after creation, like list, dict and set.
Can't be changed after creation, like int, str and tuple; operations return new objects.
Two or more names referring to the same object, so a mutation through one shows through all.
A new outer container holding the same inner objects, made by copy(), list() or [:].
Which object a name refers to, compared with is and shown by id().
Whether a value acts as True or False in a condition. None, 0 and empty containers are falsy in Python.
Python's single "no value" object, returned by functions that end without return.

summary: Variables are names bound to values; y = x binds a second name and never copies.
Ints are exact, floats approximate: compare with math.isclose() and keep money in cents.
Convert explicitly; int() truncates toward zero and bool("False") is True.
Immutable values return new objects; mutable ones change in place and those methods return None.
== compares values, is compares identity: use is for None, and copy lists (deeply when nested).
Empty containers are falsy in Python but empty arrays and objects are truthy in JavaScript.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to someone new to programming why appending to list b also changed list a after b = a, why the same surprise can't happen with two names for one string, and how you would make b a real copy.

questions.question: Complete the line so it prints Count: 5
questions.explanation: + between a string and an int raises TypeError, so convert the int with str(count) first. int(count) is still an int, and ints have no .str() method. An f-string, f"Count: {count}", is another fix.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: int("7") is 7 and float("2.5") is 2.5. Adding an int and a float gives a float: 9.5.

questions.question: What does int(-3.8) return?
questions.explanation: int() truncates toward zero, so it drops the .8 and keeps -3. -4 is what math.floor(-3.8) gives, because flooring always rounds down.

questions.question: The user types 9.99. What goes wrong?
choices: input() returns a float, which int() can't accept
int(price) rounds 9.99 up to 10, so total is 20 instead of 19.98
int() can't parse the text '9.99', so it raises ValueError; use float(price)
total must be declared as a float before the multiplication
questions.explanation: input() returns the string '9.99', and int() only parses whole-number text, so it raises ValueError rather than rounding. float(price) parses decimals.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so replace() returns a new string 'bat' and leaves word unchanged. The result was never saved. Write word = word.replace("c", "b") to keep it.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: sort() changes the list in place and returns None. nums is now [1, 2, 3], but result is None. Use sorted(nums) when you want a new sorted list back.

questions.question: What is the difference between a mutable and an immutable object? Give one example of each.
questions.answer: A mutable object can be changed in place after it is created, such as a list with append(). An immutable object can't be changed; operations that seem to change it, such as str.upper(), return a new object instead.
questions.explanation: This difference decides whether aliasing can surprise you and whether you must save a method's result.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: b = a doesn't copy the list; both names refer to one list. Appending through b changes that list, so a also has 3 items.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
def add_item(items):
    items.append("x")

cart = []
add_item(cart)
add_item(cart)
print(cart)
questions.explanation: Passing cart to the function makes items an alias for the same list. Each call appends to that one list, so it ends with two items. The function doesn't need to return anything for the change to stick.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: == compares values, and both lists hold the same items, so it is True. is checks identity, and these are two separate list objects, so it is False.

questions.question: Complete the line so backup is an independent copy that doesn't change when scores changes.
questions.code:
scores = [90, 85]
backup = _____
scores.append(70)
print(backup)   # should print [90, 85]
questions.explanation: scores.copy() builds a new list with the same items. backup = scores would only create an alias, so backup would show 70 too. Lists have no clone() method, and [scores] is a new list whose single item is the original list.

questions.question: This should change only the top-left cell, but every row changes. Why?
choices: grid[0][0] refers to a whole column, not one cell
[0] * 3 creates a tuple, which can't be changed
The outer * 3 repeats a reference to one inner list; build rows with [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
Nested lists must be created with the list() function
questions.explanation: * on a list copies references, not the objects inside, so all three rows are one shared list and a change through grid[0] shows in every row. The comprehension creates a new inner list on each pass. [0] * 3 itself is fine, because ints are immutable.

questions.question: Which group contains only falsy values?
questions.explanation: Zero, the empty string, the empty list and None are all falsy. "0" and "False" are non-empty strings, and [0] is a list with one item, so all three are truthy.

questions.question: Why does this crash for the code HELLO?
choices: find_discount returns None when the code doesn't match, and 100 - None raises TypeError; add return 0 at the end
The function needs an else branch, or Python raises SyntaxError
discount is a string, so it must be cast with int() first
questions.explanation: When the if is false, the function reaches its end without a return, so it returns None. Subtracting None from an int raises TypeError. An else is optional; the real fix is to return a number on every path.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: or returns its first truthy operand. The empty string is falsy, so the expression evaluates to "Guest". If name were "Ana", it would print Ana.

questions.question: Complete the condition so it compares the two floats safely.
questions.explanation: math.isclose() returns True when two floats are equal within a small tolerance, which absorbs rounding errors like 0.30000000000000004. total == 0.3 would be False. The other names don't exist in the math module.

questions.question: Which line prints the mathematically exact result?
questions.explanation: Ints have unlimited precision, so 2 ** 100 is exact. 0.1 + 0.7 prints 0.7999999999999999 and 1.1 * 3 prints 3.3000000000000003. Converting 2 ** 53 + 1 to a float loses the final 1, because floats can't represent every integer that large.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
x = 5
y = x
x = x + 1
print(x, y)
questions.explanation: y = x binds y to the same 5. x = x + 1 creates a new value, 6, and rebinds only x. Rebinding one name never moves another.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
a = 1
b = 2
a, b = b, a + b
print(a, b)
questions.explanation: Python evaluates the whole right side first, using the old values: b is 2 and a + b is 1 + 2 = 3. Only then are a and b rebound. If you got 2 4, you updated a before computing a + b.

questions.question: Which of these are valid Python variable names? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Names can use letters, digits and underscores but can't start with a digit, so 2nd_place fails. total-price reads as total minus price, and class is a keyword. firstName is valid, though Python style prefers first_name.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: bool is a subtype of int: True counts as 1 and False as 0. Summing a list of bools therefore counts the True values.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: round() sends exact halves to the nearest even number (banker's rounding), so 2.5 goes down to 2 and 3.5 goes up to 4. Many people expect 3 4.

questions.question: A settings file stores the text "True" or "False" in text. Which line turns it into the right bool in both cases?
questions.explanation: Comparing the text gives True only for "true" in any case. bool(text) is True for every non-empty string, including "False". int("True") raises ValueError, and a string is never the object True.

questions.question: Why does this raise TypeError?
choices: Tuples are immutable, so their items can't be reassigned; build a new tuple such as (5, point[1])
Tuple indexes start at 1, so point[0] doesn't exist
point must be created with tuple() before it can be indexed
A tuple can only hold strings
questions.explanation: Reading point[0] is fine, but assigning to it raises TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment. Create a new tuple, or use a list if the values need to change.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
s = "ab"
t = s
s += "c"

a = [1]
b = a
a += [2]

print(t, b)
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so s += "c" builds a new string and rebinds s, leaving t as "ab". For a list, += extends the existing object in place, so b, an alias of a, sees [1, 2].

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
copied = original.copy()
copied[0].append(99)
